Restored 1966 Chevy Caprice Looks Beautiful and Needs Nothing, Don't Trust the Odometer
27 photos
Photo: Druk Auto on eBay
This Caprice isn’t a regular full-size Chevrolet . It’s a restored car that’s here because it’s ready to sell, with the dealer in charge of finding a buyer revealing that it doesn’t need anything, and it’s ready for the road.
To be honest, this is barely a surprise. The photos speak for themselves and reveal a very good-looking Caprice. The reason why everything is in such good shape is a previous restoration. That’s right, this Caprice has already been refreshed, and that is why you shouldn’t trust the odometer.
If you get inside this Caprice, you’ll discover that the car shows 13K miles on the clock, and while that wouldn’t be such a big surprise, this isn’t the actual mileage. This is because the odometer was reset when the car was restored, as the dealer explains.
The Caprice was born in 1965, when Chevrolet tried to repeat the Impala success with a similar approach. The Caprice was the top Impala version, just like the Impala was the top Bel Air version when it launched in 1958. Just like the Impala, the Caprice also needed a single year to graduate from a version of another nameplate to a stand-alone series.
Starting in 1966, the Caprice was a series of its own, and it rapidly gained ground, becoming a very solid reason to buy a full-size Chevrolet. It had all the bells and whistles you could get in a full-size Chevy, despite sharing the look and many engines with its regular siblings. The Caprice could not be ordered with a six, as it was exclusive with V8 engines.
This specimen is powered by a 327 with a four-barrel carburetor. The engine is paired with the original Powerglide automatic transmission, and considering it’s a restored car, it shouldn’t be such a big surprise that everything is running properly. The dealer describes this Caprice as “comfortable to drive,” and there’s no doubt this is true, considering the Caprice was the top full-size Chevrolet.
Born and raised in Texas, this Caprice probably never struggled with major rust problems. However, I would still raise the car on a lift and inspect the underside, especially because no information was provided on the work it received during the restoration. The dealer claims live walkarounds can also be offered via FaceTime, so you should be able to obtain more information without going there in person.
Like any other 1966 Caprice in good shape, this specimen can’t sell for beer money, though it’s not a super-expensive full-size Chevy either. The dealer wants $22,980 for this Caprice, but the Make Offer option is also available, which is typically an indication that further negotiations are also allowed.
The listing expires in 2 days, and the car is parked in Anoka, Minnesota.
